# Postkit full documentation

Generated from the canonical Postkit guides and public package READMEs.

## createPostkit

Source: /docs/create-postkit

# createPostkit

`createPostkit` configures everything a host needs from the set of components
it actually uses: the provider, the MDX map, the directive plugins and the
manifest.

```ts
// lib/postkit.ts
import { createPostkit } from '@postkit/react';
import { article, technical, media } from '@postkit/react/kits';
import { chakra } from '@postkit/chakra'; // omit for headless views
import NextLink from 'next/link';

import { deviceDefinition, Device } from './components/device';
import { CommuneFigure } from './components/figure';

export const postkit = createPostkit({
  renderer: chakra,
  kits: [article, technical, media],
  exclude: ['Poll'],
  components: [{ definition: deviceDefinition, view: Device }],
  defaults: { Callout: { variant: 'plain' } },
  overrides: {
    Figure: { view: CommuneFigure },
  },
  link: NextLink,
});
```

## Options

| Option       | Description                                                                                                                      |
| ------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `renderer`   | The renderer that supplies the views. Pass `chakra` from `@postkit/chakra` for the Chakra views. Omit it for the headless views. |
| `kits`       | The [kits](/docs/kits) to enable, such as `[article, technical]` from `@postkit/react/kits`.                                     |
| `exclude`    | Component names to leave out of the enabled kits, such as `['Poll']`.                                                            |
| `components` | Your own components and third-party ones, as `{ definition, view }` pairs. See [New components](/docs/new-components).           |
| `defaults`   | Site-wide prop defaults, keyed by component name. See [Defaults and slots](/docs/defaults-and-slots).                            |
| `overrides`  | Per-component slot and view overrides, keyed by component name.                                                                  |
| `link`       | The link component for internal links, such as Next.js `Link`. The framework adapters set it for you.                            |

### `defaults`

```ts
defaults: {
  Callout: { variant: 'plain' },
}
```

A prop an author writes always wins. With `@postkit/chakra`, theme-variant
props (`variant`, `size`, `tone`) are written into the recipe's
`defaultVariants`; other props become the view's defaults. The same object
works with the headless renderer.

### `overrides`

Each key is a component name. Each value can set:

| Key          | Rung | Description                                                                                                   |
| ------------ | ---- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `classNames` | 3    | Class names per part, applied alongside the part names. See [Part styles](/docs/part-styles).                 |
| `slots`      | 5    | Components that replace single parts, keyed by part name. See [Defaults and slots](/docs/defaults-and-slots). |
| `view`       | 6    | A view that replaces the whole render. See [Views](/docs/views).                                              |

```ts
overrides: {
  Callout: {
    classNames: { root: 'rounded-sm border-l-4', title: 'font-display' },
    slots: { icon: InkMark },
  },
  Figure: { view: CommuneFigure },
}
```

{/* TODO(0.3.0): `classNames` under overrides comes from the SiteDocsPartStyles board; spec 03 §4 rung 3 only says "classNames per part". Confirm it lives in overrides. */}

## Returns

| Property                | Description                                                                        |
| ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `postkit.Provider`      | A `PostkitProvider` bound to this set and its overrides. Wrap your app in it once. |
| `postkit.mdxComponents` | Only the enabled components, plus prose. Pass it to your MDX runtime.              |
| `postkit.remarkPlugins` | The Remark plugins for MDX and Markdown. Directives validate against this set.     |
| `postkit.manifest()`    | The `postkit.component-catalog` v2 [manifest](/docs/manifest) for this set.        |

```tsx
// pages/_app.tsx
import type { AppProps } from 'next/app';
import { postkit } from '../lib/postkit';

export default function App({ Component, pageProps }: AppProps) {
  return (
    <postkit.Provider>
      <Component {...pageProps} />
    </postkit.Provider>
  );
}
```

## Framework adapters

The framework adapters, such as `@postkit/next`, become thin `createPostkit`
presets that set `link`. Image optimisation stays the host's job. The
low-level `createPostkitNextComponents()` export from `@postkit/next` stays
available.

{/* TODO(0.3.0): name the preset export from each adapter (@postkit/next, @postkit/react-router, @postkit/tanstack-router) and add an example. Spec 03 §3.1 doesn't name it. */}

## Headless

Source: /docs/headless

# Headless

`@postkit/react` is the headless renderer. Its views emit semantic markup,
landmarks and ARIA with a name on every part, and nothing else. You bring the
look with plain CSS, utility classes or any CSS-in-JS. There's no Chakra and no
Emotion in the bundle.

:::postkit-callout{tone="important" title="Upgrading from 0.2"}
From 0.3.0, `@postkit/react` is headless. The Chakra components that
`@postkit/react` exported in 0.2 are now in `@postkit/chakra`. To keep today's
look, install `@postkit/chakra` and change your imports. There's no
compatibility shim.
:::

## Install

```sh
npm install @postkit/react
```

It brings the definitions, the behaviour hooks, `createPostkit`, the kits, the
MDX map and the directive plugin with it.

## Set up

Leave out `renderer` and `createPostkit` uses the headless views:

```ts
// lib/postkit.ts
import { createPostkit } from '@postkit/react';
import { article, technical } from '@postkit/react/kits';

export const postkit = createPostkit({
  kits: [article, technical],
});
```

Wrap your app in `postkit.Provider` and pass `postkit.mdxComponents` to MDX,
as in the [Quick start](/docs/quick-start).

## Every part has a name

Every headless view stamps the component name on its root and a part name on
each part, along with its state:

```html
<aside
  data-postkit-component="Callout"
  data-postkit-part="root"
  data-tone="tip"
  data-size="md"
  data-variant="subtle"
>
  <span data-postkit-part="icon" aria-hidden="true">…</span>
  <div data-postkit-part="content">…</div>
</aside>
```

State follows the Ark UI conventions Chakra v3 uses, such as
`data-state="open"`, `data-current` and `data-tone`. The Chakra renderer emits
the same attributes, so selectors you write for one work for the other.

## Style it

Target parts with attribute selectors:

```css
[data-postkit-component='Callout'] [data-postkit-part='icon'] {
  color: var(--brand);
}
```

Or pass class names per part, which suits Tailwind and other utility CSS. They
are applied alongside the part names, so the two approaches mix. See
[Part styles](/docs/part-styles) for both.

## The optional stylesheet

Headless doesn't mean unstyled by force. `@postkit/react/styles.css` is a
small, optional baseline with a quiet, neutral look: structure, prose rhythm
and restrained monochrome. Every value in it is a `--postkit-*` custom
property, so you can retune it with [tokens](/docs/tokens) instead of
overriding rules.

```ts
import '@postkit/react/styles.css';
```

Load your own CSS after it, or leave it out and start from bare, named parts.

The stylesheet follows the reader's colour mode. Its custom properties get dark
values under `prefers-color-scheme: dark`, and under `.dark` and
`[data-theme="dark"]` for hosts that switch themes with a class, such as
next-themes.

{/* TODO(0.3.0): link or list the full set of --postkit-* custom properties once styles.css lands. */}

## Behaviour

Interactive behaviour, such as carousel paging, code copy, tabs and
consent-to-embed, is written once as a headless hook and shared by every
renderer. Postkit's Chakra views use the same hooks, and both pass the same
behaviour tests.

In 0.3.0 every static component has a headless view. An interactive component
whose behaviour hasn't moved into the shared hooks yet is marked `chakra-only`
in the manifest and its component page, and needs the Chakra renderer for now.

{/* TODO(0.3.0): list the components that are chakra-only at release (03 D11 consequence; Poll is likely, since its behaviour isn't in 03 §8 step 6). */}

## Who uses it

Prismark's editor previews render with `@postkit/react` and `styles.css`, so
writers see the same parts your site styles. See
[Writing in Prismark](/docs/writing-in-prismark).

## definePostkitComponent

Source: /docs/define-postkit-component

# definePostkitComponent

`definePostkitComponent` creates a component definition: the framework-free
contract for its props, its named parts and how it validates. Postkit's own
components and yours are defined the same way. It lives in
`@postkit/core/components`, so manifest tooling and editors can read
definitions without React.

```ts
// callout.definition.ts
import {
  definePostkitComponent,
  prop,
  presentation,
} from '@postkit/core/components';

export const calloutDefinition = definePostkitComponent({
  name: 'Callout',
  directive: 'postkit-callout',
  category: 'article-structure',
  description: 'A highlighted note, tip, warning, or caution.',
  children: 'mdx',
  runtime: 'static',
  stability: 'initial',
  props: {
    ...presentation,
    title: prop.string('An optional heading.'),
    tone: prop.enum(['note', 'tip', 'important', 'warning', 'caution'], {
      description: 'The semantic emphasis.',
      default: 'note',
      themeVariant: true,
    }),
  },
  slots: ['root', 'icon', 'content', 'title', 'body'],
  keywords: ['note', 'admonition', 'alert'],
  example: {
    props: { tone: 'tip', title: 'Keep the content' },
    children: 'Change the renderer without changing the article.',
  },
});
```

## Fields

| Field         | Description                                                                                                                                                       |
| ------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `name`        | The component name, used in MDX (`<Callout>`) and as the key in `defaults` and `overrides`.                                                                       |
| `directive`   | The Markdown directive name, such as `postkit-callout`.                                                                                                           |
| `category`    | The category, such as `article-structure`.                                                                                                                        |
| `description` | A one-line description for the catalog and editors.                                                                                                               |
| `children`    | `'mdx'` when the component wraps authored content.                                                                                                                |
| `runtime`     | `static`, `native-controls`, `client` or `resolver`.                                                                                                              |
| `stability`   | `initial`, `experimental`, `stable` or `deprecated`. Editors can hide experimental components.                                                                    |
| `props`       | The props, built with `presentation` and the `prop` builders.                                                                                                     |
| `slots`       | The anatomy: the named parts every renderer must emit.                                                                                                            |
| `keywords`    | Search terms for the catalog and editors.                                                                                                                         |
| `example`     | Example props and children for the catalog and generated docs.                                                                                                    |
| `email`       | `{ fallback }`, where `fallback` is `'link'`, `'text'` or `'omit'`: what the email renderer does when it has no view for the component. See [Email](/docs/email). |

{/* TODO(0.3.0): confirm the other `children` value (today's declarations use childMode 'none'), and the list of categories. */}

## Props

`presentation` spreads in the shared `size` and `variant` props. The `prop`
builders declare the rest:

| Builder                      | Example                                                                            |
| ---------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `prop.string(description)`   | `prop.string('An optional heading.')`                                              |
| `prop.enum(values, options)` | `prop.enum(['note', 'tip'], { description, default: 'note', themeVariant: true })` |

Enum options:

- `description`: what the prop does.
- `default`: the value when the author doesn't set one. It appears in the
  manifest and the props table.
- `themeVariant`: `true` makes the prop a recipe variant automatically, and a
  site-wide default for it goes into the recipe's `defaultVariants`.

{/* TODO(0.3.0): document the builders for the other prop kinds (today's declarations also have boolean, number and json) and how to mark a prop required. Spec 03 §2.2 only shows prop.string and prop.enum. */}

## What it derives

From one definition, TypeScript derives the rest with no code generation:

| Derived                     | For Callout                                |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| Prop types for views        | `PostkitPropsOf<typeof calloutDefinition>` |
| Slot union                  | `PostkitThemeSlotMap['callout']`           |
| Variant union               | `PostkitThemeVariantMap['callout']`        |
| Recipe key                  | `postkitCallout`                           |
| MDX map entry and directive | Registered when the component is enabled   |

What TypeScript can't express is generated: the [manifest](/docs/manifest)
JSON, Astro wrappers, the renderer support matrix and docs stubs.

## Views

A view reads the definition. `postkitView` (headless) and `postkitChakraView`
(Chakra, with a recipe) give the render function typed `props` and a
`part(name)` helper that applies each part's attributes, class names, slot
overrides and styles:

```tsx
export const Callout = postkitView(calloutDefinition, ({ props, part }) => (
  <aside {...part('root')}>
    <span {...part('icon')} aria-hidden="true">
      {props.icon ?? marks[props.tone]}
    </span>
    <div {...part('content')}>
      {props.title && <p {...part('title')}>{props.title}</p>}
      <div {...part('body')}>{props.children}</div>
    </div>
  </aside>
));
```

See [Views](/docs/views) for writing one, and
[New components](/docs/new-components) for scaffolding a definition and view
together.

## Defaults and slots

Source: /docs/defaults-and-slots

# Defaults and slots

Defaults and slots are rungs 4 and 5 of the customization ladder. Both keep the
component's definition, so its directive, validation and manifest entry don't
change and every existing post keeps working.

| Rung            | What you change                    | How                                                    |
| --------------- | ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| 1. Props        | One instance                       | `variant`, `size`, `tone`, `layout`…                   |
| 2. Tokens       | Fonts, colours, spacing everywhere | Your Chakra system, or `--postkit-*` custom properties |
| 3. Part styles  | A component's look                 | Recipes, CSS on the anatomy, or `classNames` per part  |
| **4. Defaults** | What authors get without asking    | `defaults` in `createPostkit`                          |
| **5. Slots**    | One part of the markup             | `overrides.Callout.slots`                              |
| 6. Views        | The whole render                   | `overrides.Figure.view`                                |
| 7. Eject        | The source itself                  | `npx postkit eject`                                    |
| 8. New          | Something Postkit doesn't have     | `npx postkit new`                                      |

## Defaults

Set site-wide prop defaults with `defaults`, keyed by component name:

```ts
// lib/postkit.ts
import { createPostkit } from '@postkit/react';
import { article } from '@postkit/react/kits';

export const postkit = createPostkit({
  kits: [article],
  defaults: {
    Callout: { variant: 'plain' },
  },
});
```

Every callout now renders with the plain variant unless its author asks for
another one. A prop written in the post always wins over a default.

Without `defaults`, every component uses its definition's defaults. The
`variant` default is `subtle` for every component.

{/* TODO(0.3.0): confirm whether site defaults are reflected in postkit.manifest() per-prop `default`, or only the definition's default is. */}

### How each renderer applies them

The same `defaults` object works with both renderers:

- **Headless:** the defaults become the view's prop defaults.
- **Chakra:** props that are theme variants (`variant`, `size`, `tone`) are
  written into the recipe's `defaultVariants`. Other props become the view's
  defaults.

Because Chakra variant defaults live in the recipe, you can also set them with
[part styles](/docs/part-styles), next to the rest of a component's look:

```ts
import { createPostkitTheme } from '@postkit/chakra';

export const postkitTheme = createPostkitTheme({
  callout: {
    defaultVariants: { variant: 'plain' },
  },
});
```

Use `defaults` when the choice is about content, and the recipe when it's part
of a theme you share between sites.

## Slots

A slot override replaces one named part of a component and keeps the rest.
The part names are the component's anatomy, listed on each component page.

```tsx
// lib/postkit.tsx
import type { ComponentProps } from 'react';
import { createPostkit } from '@postkit/react';
import { article } from '@postkit/react/kits';

function InkMark(props: ComponentProps<'span'>) {
  return (
    <span {...props}>
      <svg aria-hidden="true" viewBox="0 0 16 16" width="16" height="16">
        <circle cx="8" cy="8" r="6" fill="currentColor" />
      </svg>
    </span>
  );
}

export const postkit = createPostkit({
  kits: [article],
  overrides: {
    Callout: {
      slots: { icon: InkMark },
    },
  },
});
```

Your part receives the slot's props and styles: the anatomy attributes, the
class names from your part styles and, with Chakra, the recipe's styles for
that part. Spread them onto your root element so the part still carries its
name and still picks up your CSS.

{/* TODO(0.3.0): confirm the props type a slot component receives (03 §4 rung 5 says only "the slot's props and styles"), and replace ComponentProps<'span'> with the exported type. */}

## When to go further

If you need to change how the parts fit together, not just one of them,
replace the whole render with a [view](/docs/views). If you need to change the
source itself, [eject](/docs/eject) it.

## Email

Source: /docs/email

# Email

Your posts already have callouts, figures and footnotes. `@postkit/email`
turns the same file into an email that looks right in Gmail, Outlook and Apple
Mail, so the newsletter is never a second draft.

## Render a post

`renderEmail` takes an authored post and returns email-safe HTML, a plain-text
version and any warnings:

```ts
// scripts/send-issue.ts
import { renderEmail } from '@postkit/email';

const { html, text, warnings } = await renderEmail(post.body, {
  format: 'mdx',
  baseUrl: 'https://example.com',
});

await newsletter.send({ subject: post.title, html, text });
```

Hand `html` and `text` to any provider. Postkit never sends anything itself.

{/* TODO(0.3.0): the SiteDocsEmail board passes a `postkit` option (the site's createPostkit instance) instead of `format`. Spec 03 §6.1 has no `postkit` option. Confirm the final signature and update this sample. */}

## Options

| Option       | Description                                                             |
| ------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `format`     | `'mdx'`, `'markdown'` or `'document'` (a `@postkit/core` document).     |
| `theme`      | Optional Chakra Email theme. Defaults to the light Postkit email theme. |
| `baseUrl`    | Resolves relative links and images, such as `'https://example.com'`.    |
| `components` | Optional overrides, keyed by definition, the same as on your site.      |
| `wrapper`    | Optional layout component for the header, footer and unsubscribe link.  |

It resolves to `{ html, text, warnings }`.

## How it works

`renderEmail` parses the post with `@postkit/core`, using the same validation
as your site. It maps each component to its email view, or to the component's
declared fallback, and renders the result with Chakra Email's `render()`.

It doesn't depend on a framework. Email is rendered in scripts, scheduled jobs
and queue workers as often as in a page, so `renderEmail` lives in
`@postkit/email`, not in the framework adapters.

Email always renders in the light theme. Email clients apply their own dark
mode.

## What's supported

| Components                       | Status    | In the inbox                                 |
| -------------------------------- | --------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| Callout · Aside · CallToAction   | Supported | Table layout, inline styles, your tones      |
| Figure · Audio · Video           | Supported | Image with caption; media as a linked poster |
| KeyTakeaway · PullQuote · Steps  | Next      | Planned for 0.3.x                            |
| Stat · ProductCard · LinkPreview | Next      | LinkPreview as a static card                 |
| Footnotes                        | Supported | Numbered notes at the end, no links          |
| Everything else                  | Fallback  | Declared per component: link, text or omit   |

The status on each component page is computed from what `@postkit/email`
exports, so it can't drift out of date. Footnotes always render as end notes
with superscript numbers and no links, because in-message anchors are
unreliable across clients.

## Fallbacks

Interactive components can't run in an inbox. Each one declares what to do
instead, so a newsletter never shows a broken widget:

| Fallback | What readers see                              | Used by                        |
| -------- | --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| `link`   | A short line linking to the post on your site | Poll, Tabs, CodeGroup          |
| `text`   | The content as plain, readable text           | Disclosure, Comparison         |
| `omit`   | Nothing; the block is skipped                 | ShareActions, NewsletterSignup |

When a fallback applies, or a component is unknown, `renderEmail` adds an entry
to `warnings`. It never throws on content your site renders.

{/* TODO(0.3.0): the "Used by" column comes from the SiteDocsEmail board. Confirm each component's declared email fallback in its definition. */}

## Today's API

Until `renderEmail` lands, `@postkit/email` exports the email views and a
provider, and you call Chakra Email's `render()` yourself:

```tsx
import { render } from '@chakra-email/core';
import { Callout, CallToAction, PostkitEmailProvider } from '@postkit/email';

const html = await render(
  <PostkitEmailProvider>
    <Callout title="Before you publish" tone="warning">
      Review the destination and audience.
    </Callout>
    <CallToAction
      title="Read the field guide"
      primaryLabel="Read now"
      primaryHref="https://example.com/guide"
    />
  </PostkitEmailProvider>,
);
```

The package exports:

- Views: `Aside`, `Audio`, `Callout`, `CallToAction`, `Figure` and `Video`.
- `PostkitEmailProvider`, which accepts Chakra Email theme overrides.
- `createPostkitEmailMdxComponents()` and `postkitEmailMdxComponents`, the MDX
  map for the supported subset, for email builds that compile trusted MDX.
- `createPostkitEmailAction`, `createPostkitEmailMediaModel` and
  `numericEmailDimension`, small helpers that normalize props for email.

Audio and Video never emit native media elements, because major email clients
don't support them consistently.

## Manifest

Source: /docs/manifest

# Manifest

The manifest is the machine-readable catalog of components: each one's
name, directive, props, parts and renderer support. Editors such as Prismark
read it to offer writers the components a site renders, and agents and other
tooling read it instead of importing a renderer.

Its id is `postkit.component-catalog`. Version 2 ships with 0.3.0.

## Get the manifest

For the set your site enabled, call `manifest()` on your Postkit:

```ts
import { postkit } from './lib/postkit';

const manifest = postkit.manifest();
```

Or write it to a file from the terminal, for editors that read it from your
repo:

```sh
npx postkit manifest
```

Each package that ships components publishes a `component-manifest.json`. A
host merges the manifests for exactly the components it enabled, so the result
describes your site, not everything installed.

## What v2 adds

Version 2 keeps every v1 field and adds:

| Field          | Level     | Description                                                                                      |
| -------------- | --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `package`      | Component | The package that defines it.                                                                     |
| `kit`          | Component | The [kit](/docs/kits) it belongs to.                                                             |
| `stability`    | Component | `initial`, `experimental`, `stable` or `deprecated`. Editors can hide experimental components.   |
| `support`      | Component | Which renderers support it, computed from what each package exports rather than written by hand. |
| `slots`        | Component | The anatomy: the named parts every renderer emits.                                               |
| `variants`     | Component | The props that are theme variants.                                                               |
| `default`      | Prop      | The value when the author doesn't set one.                                                       |
| `themeVariant` | Prop      | Whether the prop is a recipe variant.                                                            |

{/* TODO(0.3.0): add a complete v2 component entry once the schema is final, and the exact `support` values per renderer (03 mentions supported, chakra-only and the email fallbacks). */}

## Support

The `support` field is computed. A component is supported in email when
`@postkit/email` exports a view for its definition. Otherwise the email
renderer applies the fallback the definition declares, `link`, `text` or
`omit`. In 0.3.0, an interactive component without a headless view yet is
marked `chakra-only` for React. Component pages show the same data, so they
can't drift from the packages.

## Version 1

v1 stays readable, and Prismark's parser accepts either version. Today's
manifest ships in `@postkit/chakra`:

```ts
import manifest from '@postkit/chakra/component-manifest.json';
```

A v1 component entry looks like this:

```json
{
  "name": "Callout",
  "directive": "postkit-callout",
  "description": "A highlighted note, tip, warning, or caution.",
  "childMode": "mdx",
  "directiveRemarkPlugins": ["directives", "postkit"],
  "props": {
    "tone": {
      "kind": "enum",
      "values": ["note", "tip", "important", "warning", "caution"],
      "description": "The semantic emphasis of the aside."
    }
  },
  "category": "Article structure",
  "runtime": "static",
  "stability": "initial",
  "support": { "react": "supported", "astro": "static", "email": "not-defined" }
}
```

The entry is shortened here: `props` also lists `size`, `variant` and `title`,
and each entry carries `keywords`, `example` and `preview`. The
`email: "not-defined"` value in v1 is a hand-written placeholder that v2
replaces with computed support.

## Validation

Source: /docs/validation

# Validation

Postkit checks authored components when a post compiles, so a misspelled prop
or an impossible value stops the build instead of reaching a reader. This page
describes what is checked today and what each error means.

## What gets checked

Plain Markdown directives are validated by Postkit's Remark plugin. It is part
of the preset from `createPostkitRemarkPlugins()`, which also enables GFM,
frontmatter and the directive syntax:

```ts
import { createPostkitRemarkPlugins } from '@postkit/chakra/remark';

export const remarkPlugins = createPostkitRemarkPlugins();
```

Each directive is matched to a component by its directive name, such as
`postkit-callout`, or by the component name in lowercase, such as `callout`.
Its attributes are then checked against that component's declared props:

| Check                      | Example                               | Error                                               |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| The prop exists            | `:::postkit-callout{mood="tip"}`      | `Unknown Callout prop "mood" in Postkit directive.` |
| An enum value is allowed   | `:::postkit-callout{tone="tpi"}`      | `Invalid Callout tone value "tpi".`                 |
| Required props are present | `::postkit-card-grid` with no `items` | `Postkit CardGrid directive requires "items".`      |

Attribute values are literal strings. Directives never evaluate JavaScript, so
they're safe for untrusted authoring environments. Each component page lists
its props, their allowed values and which ones are required.

## Strict mode

Strict mode is on by default. Turning it off only relaxes the unknown-prop
check: unknown props are dropped instead of failing the build. Invalid enum
values and missing required props still fail.

```ts
export const remarkPlugins = createPostkitRemarkPlugins({
  postkit: { strict: false },
});
```

Keep strict mode on for anything you publish. A dropped prop is a silent
change to what the author asked for.

## Where an error points

Directive errors name the component and the prop, but they don't carry a line
number yet. Your build tool tells you which file it was compiling when the
error was thrown, for example the page Next.js was prerendering.

{/* TODO(0.3.0): 03 §3.1 says strict mode fails the build "with file and line". Today's remark-postkit errors are plain TypeErrors with no position. Update this section once the 0.3.0 plugin attaches the file and line. */}

## Unknown components

A misspelled component behaves differently in each syntax today.

**In MDX**, a JSX element that isn't in your component map fails when the page
renders. The error comes from MDX itself:

```text
Expected component `Calout` to be defined: you likely forgot to import, pass, or provide it.
It’s referenced in your code at `3:1-3:31` in `content/post.mdx`
```

The second line, with the line, column and file, appears when MDX compiles in
development mode.

**In plain Markdown**, a directive whose name doesn't match a component is not
an error. `:::postkit-calout` is left as a generic directive and renders as a
plain block, so the content shows up without the component. If a directive
seems to be ignored, check its name against the component page and make sure
Postkit's Remark plugins are enabled.

{/* TODO(0.3.0): 03 §3.1 has unknown components fail strict builds. Confirm whether 0.3.0 turns an unknown postkit-* directive into an error, then replace the plain Markdown paragraph above. */}

## Props in MDX

The Remark plugin validates directives only. Props on JSX elements in MDX are
passed to the component as written, so an unknown prop or an out-of-range value
on `<Callout>` isn't caught at compile time. A few components that take JSON
data, such as `LinkPreview` and `SocialPost`, reject malformed data when they
render.

{/* TODO(0.3.0): 03 §2.3 has postkitView validate props in development. Document that here once it lands. */}

## One syntax per file

MDX reads braces as JavaScript expressions. Use JSX in `.mdx` files and keep
`:::postkit-*` directives with their brace attributes for plain Markdown
pipelines. See [Troubleshooting](/docs/troubleshooting) for other integration
problems.

## CLI

Source: /docs/cli

# CLI

One small tool for the moments config isn't enough: turning on kits, taking a
component into your repo, keeping it current, and making your own.

The CLI is `@postkit/cli`, and its command is `postkit`. It depends only on
`@postkit/core` and file tooling, so it works with either renderer.

```sh
npm install --save-dev @postkit/cli
```

{/* TODO(0.3.0): confirm the install story. `npx postkit` without a local install would resolve the unscoped "postkit" package, not @postkit/cli. */}

## Commands

```sh
npx postkit --help
```

| Command            | What it does                                      | Example                    |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| `postkit add`      | Turn on a kit or component and update your config | `npx postkit add media`    |
| `postkit eject`    | Copy a component's view into your repo to own it  | `npx postkit eject figure` |
| `postkit diff`     | See what changed upstream since you ejected       | `npx postkit diff figure`  |
| `postkit new`      | Scaffold a component of your own                  | `npx postkit new device`   |
| `postkit manifest` | Write the catalog for editors like Prismark       | `npx postkit manifest`     |

{/* TODO(0.3.0): confirm `add` and `manifest` options (which config file `add` edits; where `manifest` writes). */}

## postkit eject

Ejecting copies the view (and its recipe, for Chakra) into your repo. The
definition stays upstream, so your posts, validation and editor support don't
fork.

```sh
npx postkit eject figure --renderer chakra --to libs/postkit
```

```text
✓ libs/postkit/figure/figure.tsx
✓ libs/postkit/figure/figure.recipe.ts
✓ lib/postkit.ts   overrides.Figure.view → ./figure

Still bound to figureDefinition from @postkit/core.
Run `postkit diff figure` after upgrading.
```

| Flag         | Default       | Meaning                             |
| ------------ | ------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| `--renderer` | from config   | `headless` or `chakra`              |
| `--to`       | `src/postkit` | Where the files go                  |
| `--dry-run`  | `false`       | Show the files without writing them |

See [Eject](/docs/eject) for when to use it.

## postkit diff

After an upgrade, see exactly what upstream changed in the views you own, and
decide what to bring across.

```sh
npx postkit diff figure
```

```text
figure.tsx   0.3.0 → 0.3.2
+ loading={priority ? "eager" : "lazy"}
- loading="lazy"

1 change. Your edits are kept.
```

## postkit new

Scaffold a component with its definition, headless view, styles and tests. It
gets a Markdown directive, validation and a manifest entry for free.

```sh
npx postkit new device
```

```text
✓ device/device.definition.ts
✓ device/device.tsx
✓ device/device.css
✓ device/device.behavior.spec.ts

Use it as <Device /> or :::postkit-device in Markdown.
```

In an Nx workspace, `nx g @postkit/nx:component device` does the same with
your generators' conventions. See [New components](/docs/new-components).

{/* TODO(0.3.0): the eject and new flag defaults and outputs above are from the SiteDocsCLI board; spec 03 only gives `npx postkit eject figure --renderer chakra --to libs/postkit` and `npx postkit new device`. Confirm against @postkit/cli. */}

## Kits

Source: /docs/kits

# Kits

A kit is a named set of component definitions. Postkit's 35 components come in
six kits, and you turn on the ones your writers use. Only those components are
bundled, validated and described in your manifest.

## The six kits

| Kit          | Import                           | Components                                                                                  |
| ------------ | -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `article`    | `@postkit/react/kits/article`    | Aside, AudienceBoundary, Callout, CardGrid, Disclosure, KeyTakeaway, PullQuote, Steps, Tabs |
| `technical`  | `@postkit/react/kits/technical`  | Chart, CodeBlock, CodeGroup, Comparison, Diff, FileCard, FileTree, Stat, Terminal           |
| `media`      | `@postkit/react/kits/media`      | Audio, Carousel, Figure, Gallery, Video                                                     |
| `discovery`  | `@postkit/react/kits/discovery`  | AppearsOn, AuthorCard, LinkPreview, RelatedContent, SeriesNavigation, SocialPost            |
| `engagement` | `@postkit/react/kits/engagement` | CallToAction, NewsletterSignup, Poll, ShareActions                                          |
| `publishing` | `@postkit/react/kits/publishing` | ProductCard, SponsorBlock                                                                   |

All six are also exported together from `@postkit/react/kits`. Each component
page shows which kit it belongs to.

{/* TODO(0.3.0): Footnote and Footnotes join the article kit in 0.3.0 (03 §7, D13). Add them to the table once they land, and confirm "Kit 1" means `article`. */}

## Turn kits on

Pass the kits to `createPostkit`:

```ts
// lib/postkit.ts
import { createPostkit } from '@postkit/react';
import { article, technical } from '@postkit/react/kits';

export const postkit = createPostkit({
  kits: [article, technical],
});
```

Kits are renderer-neutral. They list definitions, and each renderer package
supplies the views for them, so the same kits work with the Chakra renderer:

```ts
import { createPostkit } from '@postkit/react';
import { article, technical, media } from '@postkit/react/kits';
import { chakra } from '@postkit/chakra';

export const postkit = createPostkit({
  renderer: chakra,
  kits: [article, technical, media],
});
```

## Leave one out

Use `exclude` to drop a component from a kit you otherwise want:

```ts
import { createPostkit } from '@postkit/react';
import { article, engagement } from '@postkit/react/kits';

export const postkit = createPostkit({
  kits: [article, engagement],
  exclude: ['Poll'],
});
```

## What a kit changes

The set you enable is the set everything else uses:

- `postkit.mdxComponents` contains only the enabled components, plus prose.
- `postkit.remarkPlugins` validates directives against the enabled set, so a
  post that uses a component you didn't turn on fails the build the same way a
  misspelled one does (see [Validation](/docs/validation)).
- `postkit.manifest()` describes exactly the enabled set, so editors like
  Prismark offer writers only what your site renders.

{/* TODO(0.3.0): confirm that an excluded or not-enabled component fails strict validation like an unknown one (03 §3.1 "Unknown components keep today's behaviour"). */}

## Add your own

Your own components and third-party packages join the set through
`components`, next to the kits. See [New components](/docs/new-components).

## Compatibility

The `@postkit/react` root still exports every component for 0.x
compatibility, and individual components stay importable for full
tree-shaking. Kits are the recommended way to choose a set.

## Views

Source: /docs/views

# Views

A view is the render function for a component. Replacing it is rung 6 of the
customization ladder: you change the whole markup, and the component keeps its
definition. Its props, directive, validation and manifest entry stay the same,
so posts and Prismark don't notice the swap.

Reach for a view when [defaults and slots](/docs/defaults-and-slots) aren't
enough, for example when the parts need a different structure, not just a
different look.

## Build a view

Build the view with `postkitView` and the component's definition. The
definition gives your render function typed props and a `part` helper:

```tsx
// lib/postkit/figure.tsx
import { figureDefinition } from '@postkit/core/components';
import { postkitView } from '@postkit/react';

export const CommuneFigure = postkitView(
  figureDefinition,
  ({ props, part }) => (
    <figure {...part('root')}>
      <img {...part('image')} src={props.src} alt={props.alt} />
      {props.caption && (
        <figcaption {...part('figcaption')}>
          <span {...part('caption')}>{props.caption}</span>
        </figcaption>
      )}
    </figure>
  ),
);
```

{/* TODO(0.3.0): confirm postkitView is exported from the @postkit/react root, and check the Figure part names against the 0.3.0 figureDefinition anatomy (today's slots are root, mediaLink, media, image, figcaption, caption, credit, creditLink). */}

`part(name)` returns everything a part needs: its anatomy attributes, its
`classNames` entry, any [slot override](/docs/defaults-and-slots), and, with
Chakra, the recipe's class and styles. `postkitView` also applies `unstyled`,
merges `slotStyles` and `rootProps`, validates props in development and applies
your site's defaults and overrides, so your view doesn't repeat that work.

## Use it

Register the view as an override:

```ts
// lib/postkit.ts
import { createPostkit } from '@postkit/react';
import { article, media } from '@postkit/react/kits';

import { CommuneFigure } from './postkit/figure';

export const postkit = createPostkit({
  kits: [article, media],
  overrides: {
    Figure: { view: CommuneFigure },
  },
});
```

## Chakra views

With the Chakra renderer, build the view with `postkitChakraView`, which also
takes the component's recipe. Parts then get the recipe's slot styles and your
system's tokens:

```tsx
export const Callout = postkitChakraView(
  calloutDefinition,
  calloutRecipe,
  ({ props, part }) => (
    <Alert.Root as="aside" status={toneStatus[props.tone]} {...part('root')}>
      <Alert.Indicator {...part('icon')}>
        {props.icon ?? marks[props.tone]}
      </Alert.Indicator>
      <Alert.Content {...part('content')}>
        {props.title && (
          <Alert.Title {...part('title')}>{props.title}</Alert.Title>
        )}
        <Box {...part('body')}>{props.children}</Box>
      </Alert.Content>
    </Alert.Root>
  ),
);
```

This is how Postkit's own Chakra Callout is written.

{/* TODO(0.3.0): confirm where postkitChakraView and the built-in recipes (calloutRecipe) are exported from, and add the imports to this sample. */}

## Keep the anatomy

Emit every part in the definition's anatomy, with `part(name)`. The part names
are what [part styles](/docs/part-styles), slot overrides and other renderers
rely on, so a view that drops one loses the styles and overrides aimed at it.

## Views or eject

A view starts from nothing. If you want to start from Postkit's own view and
change it, [eject](/docs/eject) it instead: you get the source in your repo,
already wired up as an override.

## Eject

Source: /docs/eject

# Eject

Ejecting is rung 7 of the customization ladder. It copies a component's view
(and its recipe, for Chakra) into your repo, so you own the source and can
change anything in it.

Unlike copying a component by hand, the contract stays upstream. An ejected
`Figure` still imports `figureDefinition` from `@postkit/core`, so its
directive, validation and manifest entry don't fork, and your posts, Prismark
and the email renderer keep treating it as a Figure.

## Eject a component

```sh
npx postkit eject figure --renderer chakra --to libs/postkit
```

```text
✓ libs/postkit/figure/figure.tsx
✓ libs/postkit/figure/figure.recipe.ts
✓ lib/postkit.ts   overrides.Figure.view → ./figure

Still bound to figureDefinition from @postkit/core.
Run `postkit diff figure` after upgrading.
```

The CLI copies that renderer's view, plus the recipe for Chakra, and registers
the copy as the component's [view](/docs/views) override in your Postkit
config.

| Flag         | Default       | Meaning                             |
| ------------ | ------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| `--renderer` | from config   | `headless` or `chakra`              |
| `--to`       | `src/postkit` | Where the files go                  |
| `--dry-run`  | `false`       | Show the files without writing them |

{/* TODO(0.3.0): confirm the flag defaults above (taken from the SiteDocsCLI board, not spec 03), how the CLI finds "your config", and the exact output format. */}

## What stays upstream

| Ejected into your repo | Stays in Postkit                                      |
| ---------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| The view               | The definition: props, directive, anatomy, validation |
| The recipe (Chakra)    | Behaviour, such as carousel paging or code copy       |
|                        | The manifest entry                                    |

Behaviour lives in `@postkit/core/behaviors` and the renderer's hooks, so an
ejected interactive component keeps getting behaviour fixes when you upgrade.

## Keep up with upstream

After an upgrade, `postkit diff` shows what changed upstream in the views you
own, so you can decide what to bring across:

```sh
npx postkit diff figure
```

```text
figure.tsx   0.3.0 → 0.3.2
+ loading={priority ? "eager" : "lazy"}
- loading="lazy"

1 change. Your edits are kept.
```

## Before you eject

Ejecting is the last step before writing your own component. Most changes fit
lower on the ladder, where upgrades land without a diff:

- A different look: [Part styles](/docs/part-styles).
- Different defaults, or one part swapped: [Defaults and slots](/docs/defaults-and-slots).
- A new structure written from scratch: [Views](/docs/views).

See [CLI](/docs/cli) for every command.

## New components

Source: /docs/new-components

# New components

When Postkit doesn't have what you need, define it yourself. This is rung 8 of
the customization ladder. Your component is defined the same way Postkit's
built-in ones are, so it gets a Markdown directive, validation, theming and a
manifest entry for free, and Prismark can offer it to writers.

## Scaffold it

```sh
npx postkit new device
```

```text
✓ device/device.definition.ts
✓ device/device.tsx
✓ device/device.css
✓ device/device.behavior.spec.ts

Use it as <Device /> or :::postkit-device in Markdown.
```

You get a definition, a headless view, its styles and a behaviour spec. In an
Nx workspace, the generator does the same with your generators' conventions:

```sh
nx g @postkit/nx:component device
```

## Define it

The definition is the contract: the component's name, directive, props and
named parts. It's framework-free, so the manifest and editors can read it
without React. See [definePostkitComponent](/docs/define-postkit-component) for
every field.

```ts
// device/device.definition.ts
import {
  definePostkitComponent,
  prop,
  presentation,
} from '@postkit/core/components';

export const deviceDefinition = definePostkitComponent({
  name: 'Device',
  directive: 'postkit-device',
  category: 'media',
  description: 'A screenshot framed in a phone, tablet or laptop.',
  runtime: 'static',
  stability: 'experimental',
  props: {
    ...presentation,
    kind: prop.enum(['iphone', 'ipad', 'mac'], {
      description: 'The device frame.',
      default: 'iphone',
      themeVariant: true,
    }),
    src: prop.string('The screenshot URL.'),
    alt: prop.string('Text alternative for the screenshot.'),
    caption: prop.string('An optional caption.'),
  },
  slots: ['root', 'frame', 'screen', 'caption'],
  keywords: ['device', 'screenshot', 'mockup'],
  example: {
    props: { kind: 'iphone', src: '/shots/home.png', alt: 'The home screen' },
  },
});
```

{/* TODO(0.3.0): confirm how a prop is marked required (src and alt should be), whether `children` can be omitted for components without content, and what `category` a site's own component should use. Spec 03 §2.2 only shows prop.string(description) and prop.enum(values, options). */}

## Write the view

Build the view with `postkitView`, so it emits the anatomy and picks up
defaults, slot overrides and part styles like any other component:

```tsx
// device/device.tsx
import { postkitView } from '@postkit/react';

import { deviceDefinition } from './device.definition';

export const Device = postkitView(deviceDefinition, ({ props, part }) => (
  <figure {...part('root')}>
    <div {...part('frame')}>
      <img {...part('screen')} src={props.src} alt={props.alt} />
    </div>
    {props.caption && (
      <figcaption {...part('caption')}>{props.caption}</figcaption>
    )}
  </figure>
));
```

## Register it

Add the definition and view to `components`, next to your kits:

```ts
// lib/postkit.ts
import { createPostkit } from '@postkit/react';
import { article, media } from '@postkit/react/kits';

import { Device } from './device/device';
import { deviceDefinition } from './device/device.definition';

export const postkit = createPostkit({
  kits: [article, media],
  components: [{ definition: deviceDefinition, view: Device }],
});
```

Writers can now use it in either syntax:

```mdx
<Device kind="mac" src="/shots/editor.png" alt="The editor with a post open" />
```

```md
::postkit-device{kind="mac" src="/shots/editor.png" alt="The editor with a post open"}
```

## What you get

From the one definition:

- Typed props for your view, with `PostkitPropsOf<typeof deviceDefinition>`.
- A directive, validated like Postkit's own (see [Validation](/docs/validation)).
- An entry in `postkit.manifest()`, so editors like Prismark can offer it.
- Slot and variant types derived from its parts and theme-variant props, and
  the recipe key `postkitDevice` if you write a Chakra view and recipe for it
  with `postkitChakraView`.
- Anatomy attributes on every part, so [part styles](/docs/part-styles) work
  the same as for built-in components.

## Share it

A component package exports `{ definition, view }` pairs and a manifest. A
site turns it on by adding those pairs to `components`, and Prismark reads the
manifest through its per-workspace component packages setting. A component
that proves itself can be proposed upstream to Postkit.

## Writing in Prismark

Source: /docs/writing-in-prismark

# Writing in Prismark

{/* TODO(review): Ryan to confirm every Prismark claim on this page before it is published. Sources are 03 D6, D10, §3.1, §3.2, §7 and §7.1. */}

Prismark is an editor that writes the same Markdown your site builds. Writers
insert and edit Postkit components there without typing directive syntax, and
the file they save is the file your site renders.

## The same components

Prismark reads your site's [manifest](/docs/manifest), so writers see the
components your site has turned on, with their props and allowed values. The
manifest comes from the same `createPostkit` call your site uses, or from
`npx postkit manifest` (see [CLI](/docs/cli)).

Components marked `experimental` in the manifest can be hidden in Prismark
until they're reviewed.

## The same preview

From 0.3.0, Prismark previews components with the headless renderer,
`@postkit/react` with `styles.css`, bundled in its signed build. Prismark's own
renderers are retired, so each component has one rendering in the editor and
one on your site, both from the same definition.

## Callouts

Prismark vaults use Postkit's `Callout`, with `tone` as the canonical prop.
From 0.3.0, directives also accept `type` as an alias for `tone`, so callouts
written either way keep working. Prismark's Standard Callout is retired.

```md
:::postkit-callout{tone="tip" title="Keep the content"}
Change the renderer without changing the article.
:::
```

## Footnotes

Footnotes are portable from 0.3.0. In Prismark their marks show as chips, notes
are edited in place and renumber as you write, and they render in your site's
house style from the same footnote config.

## Your own components

Components you define, and third-party component packages, export a
definition, a view and a manifest. That is what Prismark's per-workspace
component packages setting reads, so your own components appear in the editor
next to Postkit's. See [New components](/docs/new-components).

## Getting started

Source: /docs/getting-started

# Getting started

Postkit gives articles a portable component vocabulary while leaving the host
application in control of routing, layout, assets, and remote services.

## Install the React package

```sh
npm install @postkit/chakra @chakra-ui/react @emotion/react react react-dom
```

Mount the provider near the article:

```tsx
import { Callout, PostkitProvider } from '@postkit/chakra';
import { postkitDefaultTheme } from '@postkit/chakra/theme';

export function Article() {
  return (
    <PostkitProvider preset={postkitDefaultTheme}>
      <article>
        <h1>My first Postkit article</h1>
        <Callout title="Portable by default" tone="tip">
          Keep the content. Change the renderer.
        </Callout>
      </article>
    </PostkitProvider>
  );
}
```

The preset gives a standalone article Postkit's visual defaults. In an existing
Chakra application, omit `preset` and pass the site's system through `system`.
Postkit then uses the host's component recipes for headings, links, buttons,
inputs, tables, tabs, code, and other primitives. Add Postkit's preset only when
its content-specific visual defaults are wanted.

## Add Markdown or MDX

Use the supplied component map with the application's Markdown or MDX runtime:

```tsx
import { createPostkitMdxComponents } from '@postkit/chakra';

export const mdxComponents = createPostkitMdxComponents();
```

Framework packages add native routing and framework-specific behavior around
this same map. Continue with [choosing a package](/docs/choosing-a-package) to
select one.

## Keep sensitive work on the server

Link previews and social metadata can require network access or provider
credentials. Resolve them with `@postkit/unfurl` in a server or build-time
boundary, then pass normalized data to the renderer.

## Choosing a package

Source: /docs/choosing-a-package

# Choosing a package

Install the package closest to the application boundary. Framework adapters
use the Chakra-based React component system and add their native routing
behavior.

| Package                    | Choose it for                                                                         |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `@postkit/core`            | Versioned HTML, Markdown, MDX, and JSON interchange without a React dependency        |
| `@postkit/chakra`          | React components, Chakra theming, Markdown directives, or a framework-neutral MDX map |
| `@postkit/email`           | Chakra Email rendering with explicit email-safe component fallbacks                   |
| `@postkit/shiki`           | Lazy Shiki syntax highlighting for Postkit and Chakra code blocks                     |
| `@postkit/next`            | Next.js MDX and `next/link`                                                           |
| `@postkit/react-router`    | React Router and router-native internal links                                         |
| `@postkit/tanstack-router` | TanStack Router and application-defined typed route resolution                        |
| `@postkit/astro`           | Astro Markdown/MDX and selective React hydration                                      |
| `@postkit/unfurl`          | Server-side or build-time URL metadata normalization                                  |

`@postkit/chakra` is the Chakra UI renderer, previously named `@postkit/react`.
The `@postkit/react` name is reserved for a future generic React renderer without
a Chakra dependency. The current framework adapters use `@postkit/chakra`.

## Common combinations

An API, feed processor, or non-React content service can use the core document
contract by itself:

```sh
npm install @postkit/core
```

A Next.js publishing site commonly uses:

```sh
npm install @postkit/next @postkit/chakra
```

Add `@postkit/unfurl` to the server or build pipeline when the site renders link
previews:

```sh
npm install @postkit/unfurl
```

Add `@postkit/shiki` when rendered code blocks need syntax highlighting:

```sh
npm install @postkit/shiki
```

An Astro site should start with `@postkit/astro`, which documents the matching
Astro integrations and component bridge.

An HTML email build should use `@postkit/email` rather than aliasing Chakra UI
to an email primitive package. It shares portable Postkit props where the
meaning carries over and deliberately changes the output for interactions that
email clients do not support.

## What adapters do not own

Adapters do not configure the application's content loader, authentication,
asset storage, secrets, deployment platform, or outer page layout. Those remain
application concerns connected through explicit component props and resolver
functions.

## Core concepts

Source: /docs/core-concepts

# Core concepts

Postkit separates authored meaning from application infrastructure.

## The content contract

Components such as `Callout`, `Figure`, `Audio`, and `LinkPreview` describe
article intent. Their declarations define names, directive syntax, accepted
props, and whether they contain Markdown children.

The versioned `@postkit/core` document preserves semantic elements, rich
component names, literal props, and children independently of any renderer.
It can be parsed from or serialized to HTML, Markdown, safe literal MDX, and
JSON. The component contract can also be authored as JSX in trusted MDX or as
literal-only directives in plain Markdown.

## The renderer

Each environment maps the portable declaration to a real component. React's
`DocumentRenderer` maps semantic nodes and declarations to Chakra-backed
components. Astro bridges the same declarations into Astro components and
hydrates only the interactive parts.

## The host application

The application owns:

- Page layout and navigation
- Routing policy
- Chakra tokens and site theme
- Media storage and URL generation
- Secrets and remote provider credentials
- Caching and persistence

Postkit provides explicit extension points for these responsibilities instead
of assuming one deployment architecture.

## Resolver boundaries

Remote content is normalized before rendering. `@postkit/unfurl` returns a
provider-neutral snapshot; `LinkPreview` and `SocialPost` render that snapshot.
This keeps remote requests, credentials, and provider-specific response formats
out of presentation components.

## Components

Source: /docs/components

# Components

Postkit includes article structure, technical content, media, discovery,
sharing, and conversion components.

Common components include:

- `Callout`, `Aside`, `KeyTakeaway`, and `PullQuote`
- `CodeBlock`, `CodeGroup`, `Diff`, `FileTree`, and `Terminal`
- `Audio`, `Video`, `Figure`, `Gallery`, and `Carousel`
- `LinkPreview`, `RelatedContent`, and `SeriesNavigation`
- `ShareActions`, `SocialPost`, and `AppearsOn`
- `AuthorCard`, `NewsletterSignup`, and `CallToAction`

## Presentation props

Portable components share compact presentation controls:

- `size`: `sm`, `md`, or `lg`
- `variant`: `outline`, `subtle`, or `plain`

Site-wide visual decisions belong in the Chakra system or Postkit theme rather
than repeated content props.

## Declarations

The declaration manifest is the machine-readable content contract. It describes
each component, its plain-Markdown directive, child mode, and prop schema.
Editors and other authoring tools can use this manifest without importing the
React renderer.

The public component explorer is generated from that same declaration source,
so it stays aligned with the renderer and editor integrations.

[Browse live previews, variants, sizes, syntax, and props →](/components)

## Markdown and MDX

Source: /docs/markdown-and-mdx

# Markdown and MDX

Use JSX declarations in MDX:

```mdx
<Callout title="Release status" tone="tip">
  The content remains regular **Markdown**.
</Callout>

<Audio src="/media/episode.mp3" title="Episode 12" />
```

Register Postkit's component map with the framework's MDX runtime. Framework
adapters supply the same components with native internal-link behavior.

## Code blocks

Fenced code blocks are automatically rendered with Postkit's Chakra CodeBlock
component. They have plain-text output, copying, wrapping, and line-number
support without requiring a syntax-highlighting dependency.

By default, non-empty blocks show `"Copy code"`, line numbers are hidden, and
long lines remain unwrapped with horizontal scrolling. Set site-wide behavior
without replacing the Markdown component map:

```tsx
<PostkitProvider
  codeBlock={{
    colorScheme: 'light',
    copy: true,
    lineNumbers: false,
    size: 'md',
    variant: 'outline',
    wrap: false,
  }}
>
  {article}
</PostkitProvider>
```

Direct `CodeBlock` props override provider configuration, and provider
configuration overrides Postkit's neutral defaults. Chakra CodeBlock defaults
the highlighting color scheme to `"dark"` when it is not configured.

Hosts that want syntax highlighting can install `@postkit/shiki`, create its
lazy adapter once at module scope, and pass it to `PostkitProvider`:

```tsx
import { PostkitProvider } from '@postkit/chakra';
import { createPostkitShikiAdapter } from '@postkit/shiki';

const codeBlockAdapter = createPostkitShikiAdapter();

<PostkitProvider codeBlockAdapter={codeBlockAdapter}>
  {article}
</PostkitProvider>;
```

`@postkit/shiki` provides practical language and light/dark theme defaults.
Pass `languages` and `themes` when an application wants a smaller or customized
bundle. Chakra loads the adapter once and reuses it for nested code blocks.

## Customize code-copy feedback

Fenced code blocks inherit copy-control content from `PostkitProvider`. This
keeps site icons and labels outside authored Markdown while retaining Chakra's
Button recipe and clipboard behavior:

```tsx
<PostkitProvider
  codeBlock={{
    copyAriaLabel: 'Copy code',
    copyFeedback: 'tooltip',
    copyIcon: <ClipboardIcon aria-hidden="true" />,
    copyLabel: null,
    copiedIcon: <CheckIcon aria-hidden="true" />,
    copiedLabel: 'Copied!',
  }}
>
  {article}
</PostkitProvider>
```

With `copyFeedback: 'tooltip'`, the control swaps to `copiedIcon` and shows the
copied label in a tooltip without changing the button's width. Chakra's default
check icon is used when `copiedIcon` is omitted. Leave `copyFeedback` unset for
the default inline icon-and-label behavior.

Direct `CodeBlock` props with the same names override these provider defaults.
Use `null` to suppress a provider label or icon for one block. Both feedback
modes announce the copied label through a polite live region.

## Configure individual fences

When the Markdown compiler forwards fence metadata through `meta`,
`metastring`, or `data-meta`, Postkit recognizes safe literal options:

````md
```tsx title="button.tsx" lineNumbers wrap {2-3} maxHeight="24rem"
export function Button() {
  return <button>Save</button>;
}
```
````

Supported options are `title`/`filename`, `lineNumbers`/`noLineNumbers`,
`wrap`/`noWrap`, highlighted ranges such as `{1,3-5}`, and validated
`maxHeight` lengths. Pipeline adapters can instead emit `data-title`,
`data-filename`, `data-line-numbers`, `data-wrap`, `data-highlight-lines`, and
`data-max-height`. Explicit attributes take precedence over the metadata
string. CSS expressions and authored JavaScript are rejected.

## Plain Markdown directives

Plain Markdown pipelines can use literal-only directives:

```md
:::postkit-callout{title="Release status" tone="tip"}
The content remains regular **Markdown**.
:::
```

Enable Postkit's Remark preset in the Markdown pipeline. Directive props are
literal values rather than arbitrary JavaScript, which keeps the format
portable and suitable for untrusted authoring environments.

```ts
import { createPostkitRemarkPlugins } from '@postkit/chakra/remark';

export const markdownOptions = {
  remarkPlugins: createPostkitRemarkPlugins(),
};
```

The focused `@postkit/chakra/remark` entry point keeps React components and
Chakra theme declarations out of build-only Markdown tooling. Existing root
imports remain supported.

## Choose one syntax per file

MDX interprets braces as JavaScript expressions. Use JSX in `.mdx` files and
reserve `::postkit-*{...}` declarations for plain Markdown pipelines.

## Portable documents and feeds

Source: /docs/portable-documents

# Portable documents and feeds

Use `@postkit/core` when an API or feed needs to offer the same article as
HTML, Markdown, MDX, or versioned JSON. The package has no React dependency.

```ts
import { parsePostkit, serializePostkit } from '@postkit/core';

const document = parsePostkit(input, { format: 'html' });

return {
  html: serializePostkit(document, { format: 'html' }),
  markdown: serializePostkit(document, { format: 'markdown' }),
  json: serializePostkit(document, { format: 'json' }),
};
```

The HTML parser keeps safe semantic structure and strips scripts, event
handlers, presentation attributes, and executable URLs. The safe MDX parser
accepts literal component tags but rejects expressions, spread props, imports,
and exports. JSON input must match the current versioned document schema.

Task lists retain checked and unchecked state through HTML using disabled
checkboxes. Markdown exports escape literal block markers, entities, and link
destinations to preserve their meaning. Footnotes are currently a literal-text
fallback: both references and definitions remain visible, but Postkit does not
generate linked footnote sections or backlinks.

## Render through Chakra

`@postkit/chakra/document` supplies `DocumentRenderer`. Semantic input is mapped
through Postkit's Chakra-backed prose primitives, so the host's Heading, List,
Table, Image, Code, and other recipes continue to apply.

```tsx
import { DocumentRenderer, parsePostkitHtml } from '@postkit/chakra/document';

const document = parsePostkitHtml(rssItem.content);

<PostkitProvider system={siteSystem}>
  <DocumentRenderer
    document={document}
    components={{
      a: SiteLink,
      img: FeedImage,
    }}
  />
</PostkitProvider>;
```

The renderer never creates arbitrary elements or invokes unknown components.
Unknown nodes are unwrapped by default, retaining readable children. Use the
`unknownElements` and `unknownComponents` props to drop them instead.

## Reconstruct rendered output

HTML serialization and `DocumentRenderer` emit versioned `data-postkit-*`
annotations by default. They identify semantic nodes, rich component names,
and JSON-compatible component props without requiring an extra layout wrapper.
`parsePostkitHtml` recognizes those hints, while also remaining useful for
ordinary unannotated RSS or CMS HTML.

Annotations improve round trips, but they are not an authenticity mechanism.
Continue to treat remote content as untrusted and expose only application-
approved component overrides and link behavior.

## Theming

Source: /docs/theming

# Theming

Postkit is host-native by default. Its semantic components use Chakra
primitives internally, allowing an existing application's Heading, Link,
Button, Input, Table, Tabs, Code, and related recipes to flow through. Postkit
adds no visual preset unless the host opts into one. The `Prose` wrapper still
provides structural content rhythm in either mode.

```tsx
import { createSystem, defaultConfig } from '@chakra-ui/react';
import { PostkitProvider } from '@postkit/chakra';
import {
  createPostkitSystem,
  createPostkitTheme,
  postkitDefaultTheme,
} from '@postkit/chakra/theme';

const siteSystem = createSystem(defaultConfig, {
  theme: {
    tokens: {
      fonts: {
        body: { value: '"Inter", sans-serif' },
        heading: { value: '"Newsreader", serif' },
        mono: { value: '"JetBrains Mono", monospace' },
      },
    },
  },
});

const system = createPostkitSystem({
  system: siteSystem,
  // Optional. Omit this when the host supplies all visual policy.
  preset: postkitDefaultTheme,
  theme: createPostkitTheme({
    prose: { base: { p: { fontSize: 'lg' } } },
  }),
});

<PostkitProvider system={system}>{article}</PostkitProvider>;
```

The layering order is:

1. The optional `preset`, such as `postkitDefaultTheme`
2. The site-wide Chakra `system`
3. The explicit `theme` supplied to the nearest `PostkitProvider`

Use content props for semantic variation and theme recipes for persistent visual
policy. `createPostkitTheme` remains the final, component-scoped override for a
documentation or editorial subtree.

Import theme-only APIs from `@postkit/chakra/theme`. This focused entry point
keeps component and Markdown declarations out of shared theme libraries and
reduces cold TypeScript work. Existing imports from `@postkit/chakra` remain
supported.

## Choose a styling mode

- Host-native: pass the site's `system` and omit `preset`. Chakra primitive
  recipes and any host-registered Postkit slot recipes control presentation;
  wrapper-owned prose spacing and semantic technical-content structure remain
  active.
- Standalone preset: pass `preset={postkitDefaultTheme}` for Postkit's complete
  visual treatment, including its dark CodeBlock, CodeGroup, and Terminal
  palettes.
- Scoped customization: add `theme={createPostkitTheme(...)}` to either mode.

Markdown headings render through Chakra `Heading` with `as="h1"` through
`as="h6"`. Postkit does not override the Heading recipe's font weight, family,
line height, letter spacing, or color. Markdown blockquotes and semantic lists,
including lists inside publishing components, render through Chakra
`Blockquote` and `List`. Code-block copy actions similarly render through
Chakra `Button` while retaining Postkit's copy behavior.

Structured controls also retain their Chakra recipe boundaries:
`NewsletterSignup` composes `Field`, `PullQuote` composes `Blockquote`, `Stat`
composes `Stat`, poll result bars compose `Progress`, and product ratings
compose a read-only `RatingGroup`.

Card-like surfaces use Chakra `Card` roots and parts where their content model
matches, author imagery uses `Avatar`, callouts and takeaways use `Alert`, and
responsive video or embed frames use `AspectRatio`. Postkit retains semantic
`article` and `aside` roots through Chakra's polymorphic rendering. Carousels
delegate paging, pointer dragging, and accessible controls to Chakra
`Carousel`, so the host's Carousel recipe flows through while Postkit retains
its article item model and content slots. Instructional `Steps` compose Chakra
`List`, allowing the host List recipe to flow through beneath Postkit's numbered
marker treatment. `Disclosure` intentionally remains native `details` and
`summary`, preserving built-in toggle behavior without client-side JavaScript.

CodeBlock's canonical content-specific slots are `title`, `language`,
`control`, `copyTrigger`, `copyIndicator`, `content`, `code`, `codeText`,
`line`, and `lineNumber`. The older `filename`, `actions`, `button`, `scroller`,
and `lineContent` slot names remain compatibility aliases.

## Tune prose rhythm

External spacing belongs to the `Prose` wrapper rather than the individual
Heading, paragraph, table, or code components. Eight custom properties provide
the default flow and internal list scales and can be changed through a scoped
Postkit theme:

```tsx
const documentationTheme = createPostkitTheme({
  prose: {
    base: {
      root: {
        '--postkit-prose-flow-space': 'spacing.5',
        '--postkit-prose-block-space': 'spacing.8',
        '--postkit-prose-section-space': 'spacing.10',
        '--postkit-prose-heading-space': 'spacing.12',
        '--postkit-prose-title-space': 'spacing.16',
        '--postkit-prose-list-indent': 'spacing.8',
        '--postkit-prose-list-item-space': 'spacing.2',
        '--postkit-prose-list-item-indent': 'spacing.1',
      },
    },
  },
});

<PostkitProvider system={siteSystem} theme={documentationTheme}>
  {article}
</PostkitProvider>;
```

The wrapper applies these defaults before its prose recipe and direct `css`
prop, preserving both theme-level and instance-level overrides. Use
`<Prose unstyled>` for a completely bare wrapper. Markdown `ul`, `ol`, and `li`
elements render through Chakra's List recipe; pass `unstyled` to a mapped list
root when its complete list subtree should be bare. Ordered-list mappings retain
native `start`, `reversed`, and `type` attributes supplied by Markdown renderers.

## Framework guides

Source: /docs/framework-guides

# Framework guides

Framework adapters keep internal links native to the host router while
preserving normal anchors for external URLs, protocol links, hashes, downloads,
and explicit non-default targets.

## Next.js

Create the native MDX component map in `mdx-components.tsx`:

```tsx
import { createPostkitNextComponents } from '@postkit/next';

export function useMDXComponents() {
  return createPostkitNextComponents();
}
```

## React Router and TanStack Router

Create the adapter's component map and render the article beneath the
application router provider. Both adapters accept a link-prop mapper for
application-specific route behavior.

TanStack Router applications can translate portable string URLs into a typed
route, params, search, mask, or preload configuration at this boundary.

## Astro

Install the Astro React and MDX integrations, add `postkitAstro()` to the Astro
configuration, and render imported MDX with `postkitAstroComponents`. Static
components remain server-rendered while interactive components hydrate at an
appropriate boundary.

Each npm package README contains the exact peer dependencies and complete
adapter API.

## Unfurling and oEmbed

Source: /docs/unfurling

# Unfurling and oEmbed

`@postkit/unfurl` normalizes metadata from Open Graph, oEmbed, OpenGraphs, and
custom resolvers. It is designed for a server or build process, not direct use
in a browser component.

## Resolution flow

1. The application receives or loads a URL.
2. A trusted server validates it against the application's URL policy.
3. `@postkit/unfurl` calls the configured provider.
4. The application caches the normalized result.
5. A Postkit component renders the normalized snapshot.

Provider credentials remain at the resolver boundary.

## Rendering

`LinkPreview` can consume a normalized link result. `SocialPost` can render a
captured social snapshot or use an application callback to resolve one at
runtime.

Live embeds should remain an explicit application choice because they can add
third-party scripts, tracking, consent requirements, and layout instability.

## API reference

Source: /docs/api-reference

# API reference

Postkit generates its API reference from the public exports of every published
package.

- [Browse the TypeScript API reference](/api/)
- [Download the TypeDoc JSON model](/api/postkit-api.json)
- [Download the component manifest](https://unpkg.com/@postkit/chakra/component-manifest.json)

Use the guides for task-oriented setup and the API reference for exact
signatures, return types, and exported interfaces. The component manifest is
the smaller authoring contract for editors and component browsers; the TypeDoc
model describes the complete TypeScript library surface.

## Compatibility and environments

Source: /docs/compatibility

# Compatibility and environments

Postkit packages are ESM-only, publish TypeScript declarations, and emit
ES2022 JavaScript. The host application's framework and build tool must support
those package conventions.

## Framework matrix

| Integration     | Supported range | Rendering notes                                                            |
| --------------- | --------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| React           | React 19        | Chakra-backed components render on the server and client                   |
| Chakra UI       | `>=3.29.0 <4`   | The host may provide a `SystemContext`; Postkit layers its recipes over it |
| Shiki           | `^4.3.1`        | Optional lazy highlighting through `@postkit/shiki`                        |
| Next.js         | `>=15 <17`      | Uses the native MDX component map and `next/link`                          |
| React Router    | `>=7 <8`        | The article must render beneath a router provider                          |
| TanStack Router | `>=1.120 <2`    | Portable URLs can be mapped into generated route types                     |
| Astro           | `>=6.4 <8`      | Uses matching React, MDX, and Markdown integrations                        |

The package manifests are authoritative for exact peer dependency ranges.

## Runtime matrix

| Capability                     | Environment                                                  |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Document parsing/serialization | Any ES2022 ESM runtime; React is not required                |
| React rendering                | Server rendering or a browser-capable React application      |
| Static Astro components        | Build/server render with no component hydration              |
| Interactive Astro components   | `client:visible` islands                                     |
| Native audio and video         | Browser-native controls; no Postkit client runtime           |
| Unfurling                      | Server, build process, or trusted editor with Web Fetch APIs |
| Plain Markdown transforms      | Node/build tooling using Unified and Remark                  |
| Shiki syntax highlighting      | Lazy client runtime beneath `PostkitProvider`                |
| Email rendering                | Build or server rendering with Chakra Email primitives       |

Carousel, CodeBlock, CodeGroup, LinkPreview, NewsletterSignup, Poll, ShareActions,
SocialPost, and Tabs hydrate as visible Astro islands. Other current Astro
bridges render statically; Audio, Video, and Disclosure retain native browser
controls.

## Repository tooling

The repository's CI and release workflow use Node.js 24 and npm. Consumers do
not need Node.js 24 merely to render browser components, but their selected
framework, build tool, and server runtime must satisfy their own requirements
and support Postkit's ES2022 ESM output.

## Stability

Postkit is pre-1.0. Public APIs are typed and clean-consumer tested, but minor
releases may refine the component contract. Pin related `@postkit/*` packages
to the same release version and review the changelog before upgrading.

## Security and trust boundaries

Source: /docs/security

# Security and trust boundaries

Postkit separates portable authored content from trusted application
